Manipulation capabilities are heavily dependent on the specific mechanical limits of a robot platform. To effectively plan for tasks, it is essential to estimate a robot's manipulability across all possible configurations. While humans and robots often share a similar anatomical layout—the torso acting as a central connection point for limbs—current manipulability estimation methods, which typically rely on the General Cross-Entropy (GCN) approach via model alignment, often neglect this specific structural similarity. To leverage this shared topology, we introduce a new manipulability estimation method grounded in the alignment of kinematic models. This approach utilizes two key technologies: ManAware-ICN, a feature-rich Instance Correspondence Network capable of accurately registering rigid bodies, and a manifold-aware operator designed to preserve the geometric variations derived from joint movements. Furthermore, we implement a linear domain adaptation technique utilizing parallel transport, ensuring computations remain confined to the local linear neighborhood of the manifold to maintain accuracy. Experimental validation confirms that our proposed framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both precision and generalization.

Using the element-by-unitarity approach, this paper investigates the production of Higgs boson pairs via channel $\text{HH} \to \mathrm{b}\bar{\mathrm{b}}\mathrm{W}\mathrm{W}^{*}$ at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This paper examines a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity within the Schrödinger equation, defined outside a smooth, bounded obstacle in $\R^{d}$ subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that there exists a critical mass threshold that splits solutions into those that globally persist and those that blow up in finite time. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a promising framework for solving differential equations by integrating them directly into the learning algorithm. However, their application is hindered by suboptimal performance and convergence issues. While sampling more data points can mitigate these problems, maintaining that sample density across non-parametric problems is often computationally prohibitive. To address this, we introduce a new adaptive sampling technique for PINNs. By identifying regions with high residual errors, and placing additional training points spatially based on a Gaussian distribution, we enhance the model. This approach is computational cost-effective while significantly improving the solution's quality compared to both standard non-dynamic sampling strategies and existing methods. We validate this algorithm on several classic physics and engineering models involving partial and ordinary differential equations, demonstrating that it accurately and efficiently resolves intricate issues. Additionally, the technique is adapted to address Integral-Differential Equations (IDEs), showing strong capability even in challenging contexts like Kostantinov's equation.

This research investigates the dynamics of self-sustained negative capacitance within Fe-doped FETs, which is driven by domain walls located in the ferroelectric barrier. We employ both experimental measurements and first-principles simulations to analyze this phenomenon. Our analysis demonstrates that the magnitude of negative capacitance scales with the barrier's thickness and local crystallographic orientation at the interface with the semiconductor. Furthermore, we utilize a drift-diffusion simulation to illustrate how this structural negative capacitance influences the fundamental operations of dual-gate devices, specifically enhancing their transconductance and amplification factors.

While the cargo software platform serves as a cornerstone for the automotive industry, its intricate composition and reliance on numerous external packages render it highly susceptible to vulnerabilities introduced by flaws in dependent libraries and mitigation failures. In response, we introduce DKG—a novel Knowledge Graph designed to automatically extract and represent security-relevant information from cargo ecosystems. Furthermore, we employ DKG to investigate vulnerability propagation within the cargo ecosystem. Our analysis reveals that a substantial majority of cargo vulnerabilities stem from issues in other packages; specifically, roughly 82% of cargo defects can be traced to at least one underlying library. Our findings also highlight numpy and scipy as primary sources of vulnerability injection into the domain. To mitigate this risk and reduce the count of transitive dependencies, we propose filtering strategies that achieve an 11% reduction in overall dependency counts. Ultimately, these practices notively lower exposure risk but may impact software compatibility and functional scope.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are recognized as leaders in image recognition, yet they have not effectively learned object orientation. Orientation Representation Learning (ORL), a method to extract direction from images, was previously proposed, but its application within DCNNs remained unexplored until now. This paper introduces Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCNs), a novel deep architecture designed for image classification that integrates orientation into feature learning. We evaluated OCN against multiple convolutional networks including VGG, ResNet, and DenseNet on the standard CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, alongside comparisons with representation learning variants of these models. Experimental results confirm that OCN surpasses conventional deep networks in performance on both datasets and that these experiments validate a stronger orientational learning capability across multiple convolutional network architectures as well as their representation learning versions.

This paper addresses the challenges of optimizing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) when processing point clouds, specifically focusing (O(mn)) graph construction costs in cases with a large number of nodes (n) sampled from an even larger point cloud environment. While prior approaches typically either restrict their scope to specific network layers, which hampers performance, they solve this problem across the entire network. Our solution involves a novel multi-stage graph construction method tailored for geometric deep learning: during pre-processing, we quickly identify a dense initial subgraph using the densest subgraph identification technique applied to randomly sampled points; subsequently, during inference, we perform sparse layer transitions by dynamically finding the densest subgraph within sliding windows of the input cloud. Furthermore, this method can leverage Approximate Nearest-Neighbors to reduce the window radius search area, improving scalability. Extensive evaluations confirm that the proposed dynamic approach is both more precise and significantly faster than current state-of-the-art nearest neighbor-based methods.

This paper presents a new semantics-based, host-independent Trojan attack that differs from existing attacks which rely on either specific target sites or large on-host cookie jars for classification. Instead, this proposed Trojan operates without a traditional cookie jar and remains entirely host-independent, meaning it functions regardless of the range of web locations a user visits. Further, it preserves user anonymity by never transmitting collected site logs to external parties. Unlike prior semantic attacks sensitive to site content ranges, this method works effectively across any spectrum of hosted content. Additionally, it maintains user privacy even when site categorization errors occur during the training or inference process. Technically, this approach utilizes concept networks to model browsing behavior; these graphs represent concepts as nodes and user interactions between them as edges, capturing the full sequence of a user's site explorations. Matching attacks are executed via concept extraction from browser history and pattern identification against these pre-established networks, with performance evaluations confirming both the viability and robustness of this new semantic attack framework, which offers distinct advantages over current methodologies.

At the Las Campanas Observatory, a V4B Magellan Baade mode camera has been adapted with a new device: the ROSIE Low Resolution Surface Photometer and Imaging Experiment Integration Field Unit. Comprising 130 laser ablated, boron nitride-coated HgII absorbance slits, ROSIE transforms ImCS from a standard imager into one capable of medium-resolution integral field unit (IFU) observations. This capability enables simultaneous spectral analysis of over a hundred individual stars, making ROSIE particularly effective for studying chemical abundances and determining ages and metallicities in old populations, particularly within dwarf spheroidal galaxies. Resolving individual stars, ROSIE offers superior stellar density sampling compared to IFF instrumentation, thereby reducing complexities related to atmospheric turbulence and spectral dispersion. Given that HgII line strengths vary significantly across different surface brightness levels, ROSIE is ideally suited for large-scale surveys targeting diverse line strength regimes. Furthermore, because such adaptations are highly cost-effective, rosie serves as an exemplary modification for other facilities seeking comparable IFF performance.

A high-resolution spectroscopic survey was conducted on 21 of the most well-characterized terrestrial exoplanets, utilizing data from the VLT/UVES and Keck/DEIMOS instruments. This study provides a comprehensive dataset of high-quality stellar spectra and determines their abundances for 13 elements. Comparing these new measurements with our previously published catalog for similar stars (Hinkel et al. 2015, A&A  581, 84), which included 31 additional stars, the current sample now spans a metallicity range of +0.10 to +0.33 dex. We analyze correlations between observed abundances and the compositions of rocky planets, finding that the trends for Mg, Mn, Ni, and Si align with random chance. Conversely, the trends for C, Fe, and Ca are more statistically significant; notably, the carbon-silicon (C/Si) ratio correlation with the chemical makeup of the innermost rocky planet suggests a marginal but non-trivial connection. Finally, we infer the probable bulk composition of a hypothetical, yet unseen, planet within the system of HD 29430.

The behavior of a liquid film flowing along a fiber is governed by surface tension and the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, a process influenced significantly at the liquid-solid interface by slip conditions. Consequently, analyzing wavelength and growth dynamics provides a viable method for quantizing slip characteristics of various surface materials.

We describe the discovery and characterization of a neutral gas outflow in the lensed, star-forming dusty galaxy AT2019019 located at a redshift of z = 2.09. At an outflowing velocity of approximately 1000 km/s, the material possesses a high specific kinetic energy. We estimate the total mass of the outflow encompasses 3.9 +/- 1.6 x 10^9 M_sun. The outflow structure demonstrates a biconical morphology with resolved geometry; however, the material within the lower-velocity cone displays signs of interaction with surrounding static gas.

The spread of infectious diseases is often modeled, in simplified contexts, on random graphs where an infected individual transmits pathogen to others with certain probability; however, this assumption of random contact networks frequently fails to reflect complex social structures involving households, workplaces, and other groups. While extending infection models from graphs to higher-order networks provides a more realistic framework for analyzing threshold extinction values, this creates a significant challenge: lacking an explicit spectral spectral characterization of these probabilities hampers predictable outcomes. In this work, we address an epidemiological scenario on hypergraphs where infection occupies multiple nodes simultaneously. By establishing a connection between infection extinction and the spectral properties of associated symmetric matrices, we derive clear conditions determining survival versus die-out. Our findings provide necessary and sufficient criteria regarding spectral quantities to establish these lower and upper bounds, thereby offering a tangible first step toward a comprehensive understanding of higher-order infectious spread.

Although deep neural networks are frequently applied to diverse tasks like classification and regression, they often struggle to capture complex patterns within hierarchical representations compared to simpler models. Model checking remains a core technique in formal verification due to its ability to exhaustively explore all program states and detect bugs, though existing solutions typically struggle with the state explosion inherent in concurrent executions caused by undetermined memory read/write orders. To address this, we introduce McMini, a model checker built on dynamic partial-order reduction (DPOR) that uses the C language's relaxed memory models specifically tailored for multicore environments. McMini achieves four key objectives: (1) it handles programs written under strict or relaxed (both thread-safe and unsafety) memory conditions; ((2)) it extends its DPOR framework to cover both atomic and non-atomic (mixed) access patterns; (3) it empowers users with a customizable scheduler that balances scheduling decisions between user-defined constraints and the tool itself; (4) it offers comprehensive analyses of program execution times under various scheduling strategies to identify optimal configurations. Our implementation's effectiveness was validated through rigorous testing, and our public release of the tool and its open-source repository support subsequent research, as demonstrated by comparisons with other leading model checkers.

WhatsApp currently holds the title of the world's leading messaging application, distinguished by its closed architecture and capabilities to disperse both truthful and false information rapidly. Notably, its default function allows a user to forward a message an unlimited number of times. Although this feature has become a significant conduit for misinformation, there remains no established research on implementing controls over the message forwarding process. Although some applications have begun introducing such limitations, a significant gap exists in a complete understanding of the effects and consequences of restricting how far a message can be propagated. Specifically, there is considerable debate regarding whether restricting forwarding effectively counters misinformation or inadvertently amplifies skepticism toward the platform, thereby facilitating the spread of unverified data. In addressing this gap, a series of carefully designed laboratory experiments were conducted to analyze individual behaviors and the resulting impacts while considering the interplay between an individual's network position and the cost associated with forwarding. Findings indicate that reducing the maximum forwarding distance actually facilitates the dissemination of misinformation, particularly in scenarios involving limited available information. Additionally, the study offers both theoretical and experimental insights into governing information diffusion by incorporating constraints on forwarding actions.

Federated learning serves as a widely adopted technique for collaboratively training machine learning models across multiple clients, and it simultaneously addresses the dynamic onboarding of new participants. However, traditional federated approaches are limited to zero-shot or few-shot scenarios and generally struggle when introducing entirely unseen classes. We address this gap by investigating new-class onboarding specifically within audio classification, where we apply a zero-shot method leveraging natural language prompts to accommodate previously unknown categories. In this framework, client devices locally collect natural language descriptions of these new audio classes, either natively or via remote APIs, and incorporate them into on-device training. Consequently, successful deployment requires a video classification model, where we evaluate zero-shot federated learning against a baseline. Our findings demonstrate ZSFL effectively new-classes onboarding—improving final model accuracy by approximately 10 percentage points over the centralised baseline, while also imitating the same with a reduced communication overhead compared to the centralised system.

This Letter introduces a theoretical framework designed for comprehensive optical analysis of high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeinberger (GHZ) resources. The study initially validates this methodology through complete measurements of distinct three-photon GHZ states within a tripartite quantum basis. The approach is subsequently generalized, with a full photonic hyper-entanglement and quantum Fourier transform integration. The utility of this proposal extends towards enhanced multi-photon capabilities for both quantum computing and quantum communication strategies.

This paper investigates a dual-component system consisting of an Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) and a Caulfield of Coordinated Multi-input Multi-Output (CMMISO) serving $U$ users. Due to the massive number of IRS elements, full signal processing for a large-scale system is prohibitive, so we adopt a cascaded approach to estimate channel states. Our solution employs a two-phase strategy: initially, IRS phase shifting is optimized to isolate signals for individual users, allowing for the use of orthogonal pilots to minimize interference among them; subsequently, we address channel estimation for both the IRS-to-user-link and the User-to-Receiver (MISO) direct paths using minimum mean square error (MMSE) techniques with appropriate prior statistical knowledge. Building on the MMSE outcomes, we further utilize a weighted minimum sum squared error (WM-SSE) criterion to optimize power allocation at the transmitter and adjust the reflection coefficients of the IRS. Finally, through a series of simulations, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

We analyze real-time information flows regarding COVID-19 coverage and related data in the United States. Using an extensive corpus of over 1.1 million local news articles—collected by identifying more than 1,600 domains for news reporting and advanced keyword matching—we track audience attention, case counts, and death tolls across all 3,142 U.S. metropolitan areas from March to May 2020. Our findings indicate that, while local newspaper volume showed a decline, online audience engagement with COVID-19 news rose. Additionally, we established significant correlations between levels of COVID-19 cases and deaths both within cities and across online news coverage; specifically, higher incident rates online reflect increased news reporting elsewhere. Finally, we find that an increase in reported cases within a specific city leads to proportionally fewer articles published about the pandemic in that same area.

Counting is a vital computational process, extensively analyzed in both cognitive science and mathematics. We provide the mathematical proof that, under these conditions, the network can asymptotically simulate counting. This capability validates the use of counting-based neural computations to distinguish between neural architectures with and without internal state.

Standard Bloom filters fail to determine exact membership due to potential positive false matches, with bounded Cuckoo and Cuckoo Quad filters offering similar verified solutions but often at a higher memory cost. This analysis compares the three approaches using a comprehensive set of benchmarks. Results indicate that a bounded Xor Filter operates 1.45 times quicker and consumes 36% less memory than an unbounded Bloom filter, while achieving 1.86 times the speed and 30.5 percent fewer resources compared to an unbounded Cuckoo filter.

Recent studies have demonstrated that solubility equilibria can generate surface features, such as haze or cloud layers, that transcend traditional stability diagrams based solely on thermodynamics. While these phenomena were examined on hot exoplanets via transit spectroscopy, this study investigates their potential signatures on temperate sub-Neptune mass exoplanets. We find a region within the planetary parameter space where transcendental cloud systems coexist with thermodynamically stable equilibrium clouds. Within these configurations, tranendental effects produce distinct double hump structures in the planet's transmission spectrum, whereas stable equilibrium clouds result in standard, flat transit spectra similar to those of the host star. We identify specific regions of the parameter space where these double hump transit signatures persist even if atmospheric vertical mixing is absent; conversely, mixing tends to erase these features. Ultimately, these results highlight how observing surface transcending chemistry and equilibrium clouds through transit spectroscopy can provide critical insights into the composition and physical characteristics of temperate sub-Neptune atmospheres.

This suggests that using biologically realistic models for connections may facilitate future advancements when combined with current learning techniques.

This work presents a two-stage approach designed for rapid detection and isolation of faults in systems with high-dimensional partial state measurements. The proposed method comprises two adaptive, moving-horizon frameworks utilizing finite or recursive least squares estimation. Initially, a detection stage operates in two phases: the first monitors all possible fault types while the second activates only after a fault is identified, with both relying on a detection index derived from a weighted 2-norm of the estimated regression vector's residuals. Following detection, an isolation stage determines the specific fault type by examining the peak elements in the same residual vector, while a decision is considered certain once further elements are confirmed fault-free through a defined threshold. These sections detail the implementation and theoretical guarantees for both adaptation, false detection rates, the correctness of the initial detection, and the accuracy of the final isolation decision.

Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is significantly hampered by the expensive collection of human-labeled training data. To address this, we introduce a new approach that uses few labeled samples by combining sparsely annotated data with unlabelled batches. This hybrid method leverages semi-supervised techniques to combine the strengths of both paradigms: it aims to minimize the high costs associated with human annotation while maximizing performance through effective semi-supervised and self-training cycles. We evaluate this process on two complex real-world scenarios—invoice processing and multi-page document analysis—demonstrating that our method matches or exceeds the performance of existing state-of-the-art systems.

The interface between indium antimonide semiconductor crystals and ferromagnetic europium sulfide serves as a critical component for spintronic and majoritonic applications. Using *ab initio* density functional theory, this study investigates how electronic structures at EuS/InAs interfaces vary with different Eu and As termination models. Findings reveal that regardless of the specific bonding arrangement, As states located near the valence band edge split into two distinct groups separated by an energy gap comparable to bulk InAs. Additionally, analyzing charge and spin densities indicates that Eu $f$- and $d$-orbitals primarily occupy lower energy levels, whereas As $p$-orbitals populate higher energy levels within the gap. These results suggest that an ideal EuS/InAs interface could facilitate both spin and superconductivity transport mechanisms.

We numerically investigate how different network structures shape the epidemic thresholds of the contact process, a key metric for assessing resilience against outbreaks. Presence-absence data, where information about some features is completely unknown, is common in fields like ecology and genetics, yet many clustering techniques struggle with such high-dimensional settings as the number of features matches or exceeds the sample count. The rheology of complex liquids is highly sensitive to interfacial roughness. By correlating roughness-induced interfaces with a solid within a dry foam, we measured the shear stress response to strain and demonstrated that relaxation processes follow an exponential pattern. These experimental findings were matched with simulations, allowing us to establish quantitative connections between roughness characteristics and shear stress reactions, specifically identifying a linear relationship between stress and the cosine square of the alpha over a range of strain rates. Additionally, roughness effects can be integrated into existing theories regarding stress relaxation in smooth-limited foams, suggesting that roughness impacts arise from the interactions between particles and walls combined with additional contact friction.

While deep learning has enabled the recognition of humans from a wide range of visual inputs, most research relies on static images or short clips, often overlooking what specific aspects of motion are actually necessary for accurate identification. This study examines how much movement is truly essential for dynamic recognizers by analyzing predictions from human-centered videos. Results indicate that models achieve near-perfect human detection even when video length decreases from standard seconds to fractions of a second. We further observed that identical accuracy is maintained whether the content is brief footage of a person walking or extended footage showing a desktop environment and a chair. These findings confirm that deep learning experts utilize extremely limited temporal data to detect humans and raise the question of whether such over-specialization hinders generalization across diverse applications like action recognition or tracking.

When ordinary matter interacts with dark matter via a dark photon, interactions can occur between DM particles and this mediator, leading to effects resembling monopole dark matter (mDM) behavior with milli-tesla magnetism. For light mDM ($m_{\rm DM} \lesssim 100\,{\rm MeV}$), interactions with galactic magnetic fields (GMFs) through the dark photon allow these fields to dissipate over cosmological times. Our analysis indicates that for DM masses below 100 MeV, electron-positron emission from an overabundance of mDM annihilation would significantly alter CMB thermal history, whereas gamma-ray constraints from the Fermi-LAT telescope exclude proton masses at or below 10 GeV. Additionally, burst electromagnetic radiation caused by sudden mDM coalescence at the Milky Way's center could outshine existing gamma-ray sources like the Crab Nebula or blazar 3C279; such events would violate observations assuming Mersmannian constraints allow it. Although GMF erosion remains possible for DM masses in the range of $10$ to $1000$ MeV, no completely parameter-free model currently exists to explain this bulk dark matter without conflict. Instead, models requiring fine-tuning or postulating the existence of "crystallized" dark matter states are more consistent with current data.

This study investigates the optical signatures resulting from a white dwarf star disintegrating near a black hole. The case studies focus on a $0.6 M_{\odot}$ white dwarf approaching both a $10 M_{\odot}$ black hole with an accretion disk and a $10 M_{\odot}$ non-rotating (Schwarzschild) black hole. The system's radiation flux was computed by analyzing the optical depth and the integrated energy emitted per unit volume from hydrogen Case II recombination processes. These calculations accounted for dynamic changes in the stellar environment, varying the density and temperature based on pressure and thermal conditions, while assuming a power-law distribution for the initial rate of energy generation. Current motion deblurring algorithms rooted in deep learning typically depend on either access to available optical flow or the use of paired blurred and sharp image datasets. Hebbian theory explains that synaptic connections within a biological brain's white matter evolve based on activity, specifically that synapses strengthen when connected neurons fire simultaneously. Many software platforms support runtime customization through mechanisms like command-line switches, environment variables, configuration files, or plugins. Finally, the paper introduces a framework and analysis system supporting these position and path-conditional evaluations, alongside several data-driven enhancements to the JLS language specification, furthering research into the automatic identification of configuration-related errors.

Measuring heart rate via Intermittent Beat Intervals (IBIs) has long been employed for health monitoring and disease diagnosis. Although natural language models (NLMs) have reached human-level performance in specific linguistic tasks, they remain resource-intensive and require extensive data for new applications, particularly when expanding into unwritten languages. Extensive testing in low-light conditions reveals that this strategy, along with other improvements, significantly boosts video restoration capabilities.

In a REINFORCEMENT LEARNING framework, a single model handling multiple tasks can lead to catastrophic interference, often resulting in poor performance on previously mastered tasks. Empirical results across a range of physical simulations reveal that this strategy not accelerates the learning process, it improves the quality of learned policies, and ensures already mastered tasks remain intact while new competencies are successfully acquired.

Deep Learning and Artificial Intelligence have transformed the tech landscape, generating remarkable outcomes across various applications. However, the complex, often opaque nature of these systems has fueled the "black box" phenomenon, prompting the development of Explainable AI (XAI) to make models more transparent. While XAI focuses predominantly on technical aspects, user-centric research into user needs, concerns, and acceptance remains underexplored. Addressing this gap, this study examines the specific requirements necessary to fulfill user expectations and buy-in. We begin by analyzing literature on user perspectives and concerns regarding AI, followed by a qualitative analysis of requirements identified in XAI literature. We then present initial findings and propose future pathways, ultimately introducing a future work paper (FW-PtRA) methodology to determine precise user needs. This research serves as the foundational step toward a comprehensive requirement engineering process for XAI,  ultimately setting the stage for a publication in Software Requirements Specification.

This paper addresses information leakage in deterministic source coding, establishing a fundamental framework using deterministic finite state machines (DFSM) to model codebooks and related structures from a graph-theoretic viewpoint. We introduce three graph-theoretic metrics that correspond to distinct operational scenarios in source coding. For cases where an adversary has full prior knowledge of the codebook, we define the "robustness" of a graph to determine the robust error probability; conversely, for an adversary with no prior knowledge, we define average anonymity to represent the average prior probability assigned to an adversarial guess. When the adversary possesses only partial knowledge, characterized by an adverse set of possible codebooks, typical sets, or constraints, average conditional entropy measures the risk of an adversarial attack. Representative examples, drawn from Tardos's plagiarism detection model, are used to support these definitions, which together form a foundation for future research into deterministic source coding risks.

Deep generative models are increasingly utilized as priors to guide iterative algorithms, yet most existing research relies on specific datasets with limited scope, often containing images from a single sensor or a geographic area, which restricts their application beyond those contexts. This study introduces **MrSARP**, a hierarchical deep generative prior specifically designed for synthetic aperture radar data that unifies diverse datasets and addresses two critical limitations: it supports cross-domain synthesis due to its broad dataset compatibility and explicitly models multi-scale structures. The proposed approach employs a hierarchical architecture comprising both global and local generators. The global generator creates high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs, while local generators produce detailed supplements to enhance spatial fidelity. A multi-scale self-attention mechanism facilitates the extraction of long-range dependencies across all scales to refine structure prediction, and a series of residual connections ensures higher performance. The architecture's capacity for hierarchical, multi-scale feature extraction effectively captures synthetic aperture image characteristics, and training on a heterogeneous collection of diverse datasets results in significant improvements over prior art, specifically in halving processing costs without compromising, and often exceeding, image quality.
